newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU agrees emergency aid for Credit Lyonnais.
newsitem.headline: EU agrees emergency aid for Credit Lyonnais.

text.p: The European Commission Wednesday approved emergency aid of about 3.9 billion francs ($765 million) for Credit Lyonnais but said the survival plan for the embattled French state-owned bank would take more subsidies than originally believed.
The new aid is contingent on new restructuring measures to be submitted by the French government.

European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert told a news conference that the new plan was unlikely to go through without "real and substantive" divestments by the company, which was once the world's largest bank outside Japan.
Credit Lyonnais is already benefiting from a rescue plan worth up to 45 billion francs ($8.8 billion), which was cleared by the Commission, the European Union's executive body, in July 1995.
Speaking in an unusually conciliatory tone, Van Miert said the plan had failed to live up to expectations due to the sluggish French financial markets and the bank's poor image in France.

"(Credit Lyonnais') rivals said at the time that the Commission had not been tough enough and that it (the 1995 rescue plan) would turn the bank into a 'super champion,'" Van Miert said. "We see today that that was not the case."
He declined to say how much the French authorities might have to pay for another bailout, but said it would be a "considerable figure."
EU rules on rescue aid for ailing businesses allow for subsidies to be paid if they are limited to putting a company back on its feet without harming competition.
French bank Societe Generale has challenged the commission's backing of the 1995 rescue plan before the European Court in Luxembourg.

Asked whether the commission would call for the early sale of Credit Lyonnais in return for further help, Van Miert said it was no use pushing for a state sale of the bank before it was financially attractive again.
The French government has committed itself to privatising Lyonnais by the year 2000.

The emergency aid package set Wednesday included cancellation of an obligation to grant below-market rate loans to a state-backed entity to which the bank had transferred about 130 billion francs ($25.5 billion) of shaky assets.
The bank had said that it would loose 3 billion francs ($588 million) in funding the loan this year.
Van Miert said that provided the French government formally notified the Commission quickly of planned changes at the bank, the executive body could make a final decision on the new plan by year-end.
